claims.text: The baseline is a tungsten-based high-entropy alloy produced by elemental powder mixing and spark plasma sintering without deliberate titanium addition or significant in-situ TiC.
Adding a controlled amount of titanium during spark plasma sintering will cause in-situ formation of TiC precipitates.
The resulting TiC will be uniformly distributed within grains and along grain boundaries of the tungsten-based high-entropy alloy.
The TiC precipitates will be nanoscale.
The TiC precipitates will form coherent or semi-coherent interfaces with the tungsten matrix.
TiC interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission.
TiC precipitates promote continuous strain hardening at high temperature.
TiC precipitates reduce localized strain accumulation at grain boundaries.
TiC precipitates delay crack initiation.
Relative to the TiC-free baseline, the TiC-containing alloy will exhibit greater high-temperature plastic strain.
Relative to the TiC-free baseline, the TiC-containing alloy will exhibit improved fracture toughness.
The TiC-free baseline has a higher brittle-to-ductile transition temperature.
The TiC-free baseline has limited high-temperature ductility.
Uniformly dispersed TiC is beneficial to the elevated-temperature performance of tungsten-based plasma-facing materials.
Dispersed TiC strengthens tungsten grain boundaries and resists grain-boundary migration at elevated temperature.
Fusion plasma-facing components experience severe high-temperature and high-heat-flux service conditions.
The magnitude of the plastic-strain and toughness improvement depends on TiC volume fraction, precipitate size, and spatial distribution.
The modified and control alloys will be processed and tested identically apart from the titanium addition and resulting TiC.
The hypothesis is restricted to powder-metallurgy, spark-plasma-sintered tungsten-based high-entropy alloys tested in relevant elevated-temperature, high-heat-flux regimes.

A lack of statistically significant improvement in high-temperature plastic strain or fracture toughness, or a lack of the predicted coherent dislocation-transmission interfaces, would falsify the hypothesis.
